This is due to a combination of planning rules and methodologies. A report from the External Market Monitor notes that ISO-NE has “aggressive local reliability planning criteria” and experiences 10% to 20% less congestion than other RTOs, both of which would favor transmission investments for reliability over economic needs (Potomac Economics 2023). The process to identify a reliability need takes fewer process steps than for a system efficiency project, which requires demonstrating a reduction in production costs. While production cost is used as the main metric, the ISO also considers transmission construction avoided by proposed system efficiency projects, avoided transmission losses, avoided capital costs, and reduced unserved energy as other metrics. Finally, the ISO’s tariff defines selection criteria for approving projects based on project cost (ISO-NE 2025a). There is no mechanism to evaluate or communicate quantified benefits for reliability projects. The Greater Boston Transmission Project was one of the largest and most expensive reliability projects planned in the ISO-NE, originally estimated to be $822 million (ISO-NE 2023b). These costs are allocated regionally based on load ratio share. In September 2020, an additional $188.6 million was requested to underground a 115-kV transmission line originally designed as an overhead line but was unable to secure property rights. The Reliability Committee did not recommend approval of this request, and the additional cost for the undergrounding project remains under review by ISO-NE (ISO-NE 2020). 3.2.6 MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue Projects The MISO-SPP Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue (JTIQ) projects demonstrate interregional planning and cost allocation for generator interconnection projects that would not otherwise be selected as part of the regional planning process in either participating region. 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. The JTIQ concept originated from developers that wanted to build and interconnect generation along the MISO-SPP seam but were facing prohibitive interconnection costs. In response, MISO and SPP conducted a joint study that identified five projects along the seam totaling approximately $1 billion (Figure 9). The projects are expected to come online in 2031. Figure 9. MISO-SPP JTIQ projects. Source: (MISO 2024b) The initial JTIQ study (SPP and MISO 2022b) established a cost allocation methodology for JTIQ projects similar to MISO’s generator interconnection cost allocation scheme. In this method, 90% of the engineering and construction costs are paid for by the interconnecting generators, and 10% is paid for by load in SPP and MISO in proportion to each region’s calculated adjusted production cost benefit. Of the 10% allocation to load, 7% was allocated to SPP and 3% to MISO-based production cost modeling to estimate the benefit to each region. Costs to interconnection generators would be spread over generator interconnection projects across multiple queue clusters to reduce the impact on any single interconnecting customer (SPP and MISO 2023).
